item.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

item.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha's predictive contribution (Gα) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD-HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha's carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and Gα each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen-Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and Gα can change partly independently. Results: Gα was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10^3Gα, -3.19; 95% confidence interval -5.25 to -1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and Gα each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in Gα, whereas reducing downstream input lowered Gα with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions: At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

item.title: Posterior-anterior striatal reorganization after weight restoration in anorexia nervosa is associated with remission outcome: from mice to longitudinal human study
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high relapse rates despite successful weight restoration. Altered reward processing and an imbalance between goal-directed and habitual control within the striatum have been proposed to contribute to the persistence of maladaptive behaviours, but the striatal mechanisms underlying recovery and relapse remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-species structural MRI with longitudinal clinical characterization to investigate striatal alterations associated with recovery from AN. Mice with deletion of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChTcKO), a model of maladaptive eating behaviour, showed reduced dorsolateral striatal volume compared with wild-type mice. At baseline, women with AN (n = 71) showed reduced striatal volumes compared with healthy controls (n = 30). Longitudinally, patients with AN (n = 41) and healthy controls (n = 28) were reassessed, revealing substantial recovery of striatal volumes following weight restoration in AN. Posterior-anterior putamen gradient changes differed according to subsequent remission status, with changes in the right putamen gradient predicting relapse. Striatal gradient changes were also associated with goal-directed and habitual behaviour during the slip-of-action task, response consistency during delay discounting, and circulating ghrelin and desacyl ghrelin concentrations. These findings identify longitudinal putamen reorganization as a candidate marker of vulnerability to relapse and link striatal plasticity to reward-related and metabolic processes in AN.

item.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Importance: The prenatal period is a critical window for intergenerational transmission of adversity, yet the neural substrates through which cumulative prenatal stress becomes biologically embedded in offspring brain development remain poorly understood. White matter microstructure is a candidate mechanism linking prenatal adversity to downstream emotional dysregulation. Objective: To examine associations between cumulative adverse prenatal exposure (APE) burden and fronto-limbic white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) at baseline and across adolescent developmental trajectories, and to test whether white matter FA mediates prenatal APE effects on emotional dysregulation. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cohort study using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 7.0, a diverse longitudinal cohort of US children recruited at ages 9 to 10 years across 21 sites. After diffusion tensor imaging quality control exclusions and retention of one twin or triplet per family, the final cross-sectional analytic sample comprised 10 483 participants. Longitudinal analyses included participants with data at one or more follow-up timepoints across four imaging waves. Exposures: Cumulative APE burden, operationalized as a sum of six binary adverse prenatal exposures (unplanned pregnancy; early alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use before pregnancy recognition; complicated pregnancy; complicated birth; range, 0-6) following Zhi et al. (2026). Main Outcomes and Measures: Fractional anisotropy in 11 a priori fronto-limbic white matter tracts at baseline (ages approximately 10 years) and across four imaging timepoints (ages approximately 10, 12, 14, and 16 years). Exploratory outcomes included Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) dysregulation profile and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) subscales. Results: Higher prenatal APE burden was associated with lower baseline FA in left uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00096; 95% CI, −0.00151 to −0.00042; FDR-corrected P = .006), corpus callosum (b = −0.00079; 95% CI, −0.00125 to −0.00032; FDR-corrected P = .006), and right uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00071; 95% CI, −0.00120 to −0.00021; FDR-corrected P = .019). These associations were robust to adjustment for diffusion image quality, and prenatal burden was not associated with baseline image quality. In repeated-measures models across four imaging timepoints, higher APE burden was associated with steeper FA increases across adolescence (positive APE x Age interaction in 5 of 11 tracts; positive across all 11), though these trajectory effects were attenuated after adjustment for image quality. Post hoc analyses indicated that pregnancy complications and prenatal cannabis exposure were the most consistent contributors to these associations. White matter FA partially mediated the association between prenatal APE burden and involuntary emotional dysregulation, with no association with voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Conclusions and Relevance: Cumulative prenatal APE burden was associated with lower fronto-limbic white matter FA at the start of adolescence, an association that was stable across development and robust to image-quality adjustment. Evidence for altered developmental trajectories was more sensitive to image quality and should be interpreted cautiously. These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter-- particularly the uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum-- as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, while underscoring that this pathway reflects a bounded set of prenatal exposures.

item.title: Proteogenomics captures a midlife biological state of Alzheimer's disease susceptibility
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Alzheimer's disease (AD) develops over decades, but biological processes underlying susceptibility during midlife remain poorly understood. Using multimodal neuroimaging and plasma proteomics in UK Biobank participants, we identified circulating proteomic signatures of brain structure and organization. This 'neurostructural proteome' predicted future cognitive decline, incident dementia, and later-life AD pathology across independent cohorts spanning two decades of follow-up. Genetic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses demonstrated convergence of the neurostructural proteome and AD genetic architecture, highlighting enrichment in astrocyte, microglia, and endothelial pathways beyond the APOE region. Collectively, these findings identify a circulating neurostructural proteome detectable in midlife that captures molecular processes associated with future AD susceptibility and provide a framework for uncovering an early biological landscape of disease susceptibility that precedes conventional biomarkers and clinical onset.

item.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

item.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

item.title: Shared control-network recruitment and task-dependent brain-behavior associations in bilingual language and rule switching.
item.description:
Cognitive, affective & behavioral neuroscience
Bilingual language control is thought to draw on domain-general cognitive control, yet it remains unclear whether cross-task overlap in neural recruitment is accompanied by similar brain-behavior relationships. Previous connectivity studies have typically estimated functional connectivity (FC) across entire tasks or blocks, obscuring network changes specific to switch trials. We combined hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling, regional activation, and beta-series FC in 126 Chinese-English bilinguals (123 with usable fMRI data) who completed language- and rule-switching tasks. Both tasks reduced drift rates and prolonged nondecision times on switch trials. They also recruited a common 28-region switch-sensitive control core and showed increased switch-related FC within this core and between the core and default mode, subcortical, and cerebellar systems. At the individual-difference level, generalized estimating equations revealed task-dependent brain-behavior relationships: core-within and core-subcortical FC were more positively associated with drift-rate switch cost during language switching than during rule switching. Together, the results identify partial overlap in regional recruitment, similarly directed system-level FC changes, and distinct FC-evidence-accumulation relationships across tasks.

item.title: Hidden Neural Variability and the Unexplained Cochlear Implant Outcome
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Cochlear implants work, but not equally. After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained. Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear. Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device. This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance. It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged. Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.

item.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

item.title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual "Cocktail-party" paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding-decoding analyses. Participants (18 female, 14 male) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated mid-latency (100 - 250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270 - 450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory-language processing during selective listening of continuous speech.Significance Statement Understanding how the brain prioritizes and selectively processes information in naturalistic, continuously evolving audiovisual scenes such as conversations is a central challenge in neuroscience. Here, we show that conversations conveying negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant content enhance neural tracking of attended speech in a noisy cocktail-party setting. This enhanced tracking depends on the semantic structure of the conversation, emerging earlier for coherent dialogues that are easy to follow. Furthermore, we show that emotional content strengthens mechanisms related to speech comprehension and sharpens segregation of relevant from irrelevant talk. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning and semantic continuity jointly shape cortical processing of continuous speech, providing new insight into how the brain selects and processes meaningful information during a conversation.

item.title: Neurocognitive characteristics of perceptual feedback processing differ in autism.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Autistic individuals often show reduced adaptation to changing environmental demands, but the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We asked whether it may be explained by reduced sensitivity to external feedback and changes in task difficulty. Autistic and non-autistic adults of either sex, matched for cognitive ability, performed a pitch discrimination task in which their response was immediately followed by feedback. Accuracy was similar between the two groups, yet autistic participants exhibited a markedly reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an event-related EEG potential differentiating explicit negative versus positive feedback. They also showed weaker modulation of feedback-evoked EEG responses by perceptual difficulty. Lastly, they showed reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up experiment conducted 1-2 years later. When combined they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with about 80% accuracy. Together, our findings indicate that multiple processes for evaluating perceptual decisions and adjusting subsequent behavior differ in autism and likely contribute to slow updating in changing contexts.Significance Statement Autism is associated with reduced adaptation to changing environments in both behavior and neural signals, but the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that autistic individuals exhibit a reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an EEG component that is present when receiving negative instead of positive feedback. They also show weaker neural modulation by perceptual difficulty and reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up study. When combined, they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with high accuracy. These findings suggest that reduced flexibility in autism is associated with reduced processing of external feedback and task difficulty.

item.title: Repeated Head Impacts May Compromise White Matter Integrity and Bimanual Coordination in American Football Players.
item.description:
Sports health
Background Repeated head impacts (RHI) in American Football may contribute to subtle white matter (WM) abnormalities and functional deficits even in the absence of clinically diagnosed concussion. Hypothesis Contact athletes would demonstrate tract-specific differences in fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) compared with noncontact controls, and high-exposure (HE) athletes would show greater within-season diffusion change, worse bimanual coordination, and greater symptom burden than low-exposure (LE) athletes. Study design Prospective cohort study. Level of evidence Level 3. Methods Twenty-two male varsity American Football players and 13 male noncontact controls underwent preseason diffusion tensor imaging. Football athletes were monitored over a single season using helmet-mounted accelerometers and stratified into HE and LE groups. Tract-specific FA and MD were derived using probabilistic tractography. Pre-post SCAT3 symptom and severity checklist data were collected from all football athletes, and pre-post Kinarm Ball-on-Bar (BOB) bimanual coordination data were available for 12 athletes. Results At preseason, contact athletes demonstrated higher FA in 15 of 16 tracts compared with noncontact controls, with lower FA in the forceps minor. MD was lower in 10 of 16 tracts, higher in the bilateral inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and similar in the corticospinal tract and superior thalamic radiation. Over the season, HE athletes sustained more impacts (P < 0.001) and greater cumulative g -force (P = 0.001) than LE athletes. On the BOB task, LE athletes showed modest improvement, whereas HE athletes worsened, yielding a between-group difference in change of 0.59 (95% CI, 0.22-0.96; P = 0.005). Generalized estimating equation models accounting for within-athlete tract correlations did not detect HE-versus-LE differences in FA change (Wald χ²(1) = 0.14; P = 0.71) or MD change (Wald χ²(1) < 0.01; P > 0.99), and SCAT3 symptom and severity scores remained low with no meaningful between-group differences. Conclusion In 22 contact athletes, repeated head-impact exposure was associated with preseason WM differences and worsening bimanual coordination across a single season, while longitudinal tract-level DTI and symptom-based clinical measures showed limited between-group change. Clinical relevance Objective motor assessment and advanced neuroimaging may help characterize subtle consequences of RHIs that are missed by routine symptom-based tools.

item.title: Targeting central thalamus with transcranial ultrasound reduces arousal in healthy volunteers.
item.description:
Communications biology
Using low-intensity focused transcranial ultrasound stimulation, we test the causal roles of the central thalamus in arousal and the pulvinar in visuospatial attention in the healthy human brain. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced design, 27 healthy volunteers (two females) complete a vigilance task (Psychomotor Vigilance Task) and a visuospatial attention task (Egly-Driver Task) before and after sham, central thalamic, and pulvinar sonication. Targeting the central thalamus slows responses and increases lapses in attention during the vigilance task, indicating reduced arousal. Pulvinar sonication reduces (and slows) responses to visual stimuli presented contralaterally, suggesting a disruption of contralateral visuospatial attention. These results provide causal evidence linking the pulvinar to visuospatial attention and the central thalamus to arousal in the healthy human brain and demonstrate that ultrasound can elicit distinct behavioral changes in healthy volunteers when delivered to close but functionally distinct thalamic regions, underscoring its potential as a tool for noninvasive brain mapping.

item.title: Neural limits of temporal feature binding in human visual cortex.
item.description:
Nature communications
Humans are able to track the change of color and orientation (CO) of an object at a stunning rate. However, spatially separating those features slows this rate by an order of magnitude - a temporal limit of feature binding that is little understood. Here, we investigate the underlying mechanisms using high-temporal resolution cortical source localization of the magnetic field response elicited by CO-pairs alternating at different frequencies in color and orientation. We show that (1) binding requires a rapid recurrent modulation (~120 ms) of activity in V1/V2, whose latency is independent of the alternation rate. (2) Performance drops to chance when the alternation rate becomes too high to accommodate the recurrent process within a single alternation. (3) CO binding itself is mediated by color-based attention, which gradually biases re-occurring CO combinations containing the attended color. These observations together demonstrate that CO-binding across space depends on rapid recurrent processing in early visual cortex, with its temporal limit being set by the time this process takes to be completed. Binding ultimately results from a slower and gradual attentional bias of the recurrent process instantiating a form of stroboscopic stationarity in the stream of alternations for unambiguous discrimination of the correct feature-combination.

item.title: Low-dose ketamine modulates brain entropy in treatment-resistant depression: Results from two neuroimaging clinical trials.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background Several studies have reported entropy reductions in regions of the brain associated with affective-regulatory and reward- and motivation-related processes in patients with major depressive disorder. However, whether low-dose ketamine modulates this reduction remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from two single-infusion low-dose ketamine trials. Data at baseline and 3 days after infusion were analyzed. In Trial 1, patients with treatment-resistant depression were randomized to receive 0.2 or 0.5 mg/kg ketamine or normal saline. In Trial 2, patients with treatment-resistant depression and suicidal ideation were randomized to receive either 0.5 mg/kg ketamine or 0.045 mg/kg midazolam. Sample entropy was calculated from the spontaneous blood oxygenation level-dependent time series of 166 regions of interest defined by the automated anatomical labeling atlas 3. Results In Trial 1, increased brain entropy was observed in the gyrus rectus, cerebellar vermis I/II, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and bilateral locus coeruleus after low-dose ketamine infusion. In Trial 2, the ketamine group exhibited higher brain entropy in the left amygdala compared with the midazolam group. Discussion Low-dose ketamine rapidly increases brain entropy (from baseline to day 3) in frontolimbic, cerebellar, and ascending neuromodulatory regions, including the gyrus rectus, cerebellar vermis I/II, substantia nigra, red nucleus, bilateral locus coeruleus, and left amygdala. Changes in brain entropy after low-dose ketamine infusion may be associated with its rapid antidepressant and antianhedonic effects, although this relationship requires further investigation.

item.title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation.
item.description:
Current biology : CB
Knowing which way you are facing is essential for navigation. In animals, a dedicated set of neurons-head direction cells-acts as an internal compass: each cell fires most strongly when the animal faces a particular direction. The anterior thalamus is a key hub for this system. In humans, however, direct electrophysiological evidence for a comparable head direction signal remains limited. To address this gap, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) from the anteroventral thalamus (AVT) in patients with epilepsy while they performed a virtual navigation task. We analyzed neural activity during in-place rotation to isolate virtual head direction (vHD) information. Using inverted encoding models applied to multi-band neural activity, we reconstructed continuous vHD within two distinct virtual environments. Critically, the decoders failed to generalize across environments, indicating that the AVT vHD representation is environment specific rather than a fixed, universal map. This encoding was observed in the AVT and was temporally specific to rotation epochs; no significant encoding was detected in the pulvinar, another thalamic subregion not part of the classic head direction network in rodents. Together, these findings suggest that the human AVT carries environment-specific vHD information, bridging a gap between animal models and human navigation and highlighting a potential link to spatial disorientation disorders.

item.title: High-Intensity Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation for Post-Stroke Cognitive Impairment: A Triple-Blind Randomized Trial.
item.description:
Brain stimulation
Background Non-invasive neuromodulation for post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) holds promise, but high-level evidence is lacking, partly due to the challenge of targeting single brain regions in a condition with diverse lesions and multi-network dysfunction. Objective The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of high-intensity transcranial alternating current stimulation (Hi-tACS) on cognitive function in patients with PSCI. Methods In this triple-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial, PSCI patients were randomized to receive either active or sham Hi-tACS. The tACS group received active Hi-tACS at 15 mA and 77.5 Hz for 40 minutes, twice daily, 5 days a week for 2 weeks. The sham group used identical devices without current delivery. The primary outcome was the change in Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score. Secondary outcomes included Digit Span Test and cerebral oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentration changes measured by functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Results The tACS group (n=34) showed higher MoCA response rates than the sham group (n=34) immediately after treatment (73.5% vs 38.2%, P=0.003) and at the 4-week post-treatment follow-up (88.2% vs 55.9%, P=0.003). Improvements in forward and backward digit span were also greater in the tACS group at both assessments. The intention-to-treat analysis of all 70 randomized participants yielded results consistent with the per-protocol analysis. Exploratory fNIRS analyses identified greater HbO increases in the left, right, and medial prefrontal regions in the tACS group at T1 after FDR correction (all q=0.033), whereas no regional difference remained significant at T2. Conclusion Hi-tACS improved global cognition and working memory in patients with PSCI and was generally well tolerated. Exploratory fNIRS findings suggested possible accompanying changes in cortical activation and network organization but did not establish a neurophysiological mechanism. Importantly, as a broad-network stimulation approach, Hi-tACS may reduce reliance on selecting a single precise target, a potential practical advantage in heterogeneous PSCI.

item.title: A Sensorimotor-Interoceptive Model for Sensory Phenomena in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Neural and Computational Mechanisms.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Classical models of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) grounded in cognitive-affective processes do not fully account for sensory phenomena (SP), including bodily discomfort, incompleteness, and not-just-right experiences that often precede or accompany compulsive behavior. To address this gap, we propose a sensorimotor-interoceptive model for the sources, generation, and maintenance of SP and SP-driven compulsions in OCD. Specifically, the posterior insula may integrate external sensory signals with internal bodily signals within the perceptual module. These integrated signals are subsequently processed by the salience module centered on the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex, where heightened error monitoring may assign excessive salience to integrated signals and recruit the supplementary motor area and primary motor cortex to initiate corrective actions. Dysfunction of a cerebellum-centered forward system may then produce persistent mismatches between predicted and actual action outcomes, which are re-entered into the perceptual module and sustain a recurrent feedback loop. The framework therefore conceptualizes SP-driven compulsions as maladaptive attempts to resolve persistent sensory errors. Predictive coding and active inference provide a computational account of these processes. We underscore that this sensorimotor-interoceptive model, intended to complement existing models, provides an account of symptoms in which SP are prominent and may therefore contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of OCD.

item.title: Histological morphometric correlates of MRI-defined cortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Large-scale MRI studies have consistently demonstrated progressive and age-accelerated neocortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These findings are frequently interpreted as evidence of cumulative neurodegeneration. However, the histopathological substrates underlying MRI-confirmed cortical thinning in epilepsy remain poorly defined. In particular, it is unknown whether cortical thinning reflects irreversible neuronal loss or potentially reversible epilepsy-related network alterations in cortical microstructure. We analysed the resected middle temporal gyrus from 117 individuals undergoing surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy, including cases with (n= 74) or without hippocampal sclerosis (HS) and 12 cases with additional temporal lobe sclerosis (TLS, or Focal Cortical Dysplasia IIIa), defined by a distinct pattern of cytoarchitectural reorganisation and gliosis involving superficial layers. All cases were stratified by the presence or absence of pre-operative MRI-defined cortical thinning of the middle temporal gyrus, quantified using CAT12 relative to healthy controls. On NeuN-immuno-labelled sections using automated image analysis we assessed neuronal spatial distributions relative to their size and packing density; relative cortical layer thickness and sulcal-gyral cytoarchitectural variation were also quantified. MRI-defined cortical thinning was not associated with diffuse neuronal loss. Instead, thinning correlated with increased neuronal density and altered cell-size spatial organisation in superficial and deep layers, particularly in right temporal lobe epilepsy cases with HS. There was limited evidence of layer-specific laminar thinning, being confined to layer VI in the right TLE/HS group only. Of note, TLS cases did not show either cortical thinning on MRI or laminar thinning on histology compared to cases without TLS but altered neuronal densities and composition that was not confined to the superficial cortex. MRI cortical thinning was also characterised by attenuation of normal sulcal/gyral cytoarchitectural variations suggesting disruption of cortical architectural gradients. In contrast, cases with HS but without MRI cortical thinning demonstrated loss of the expected inter-hemispheric cytoarchitectural asymmetry, indicating a distinct pathological process dissociated from thinning. Clinical-pathological correlations were lateralised, including age of onset, further supporting distinct mechanisms contributing to MRI cortical thinning between left and right TLE. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MRI-defined cortical thinning in epilepsy reflects progressive neuronal degeneration. Rather than laminar neuronal loss and atrophy, thinning was associated with altered neuronal packing and cell-size distributions between layers. This points towards altered neuropil volumes, including myelin content and dendritic remodelling, in turn suggesting potentially reversible dynamic seizure- or network-related processes.

item.title: Cellular and mitochondrial correlates of regional glucose metabolism in the human cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Regional differences in human brain glucose metabolism reflect local energy demands, but their cellular and mitochondrial determinants remain unclear. We combined [18F]FDG positron emission tomography in healthy human participants with estimates of cellular composition and mitochondrial density to unravel (sub)cellular correlates of heterogeneity in brain glucose metabolism. By correcting for RNA content and differential gene expression due to postmortem sampling, we addressed methodological shortcomings in multimodal neuroimaging integration. We introduce transcriptionally derived cytoarchitectonic maps of the human cortex that are consistent with histological findings, providing a biologically grounded framework for relating in vivo neuroimaging signals. Accordingly, mitochondrial distribution showed strong association with the intrinsic energy requirements at resting state. In contrast, relations between metabolism and neuronal composition were driven by sensory input and mitochondria-sparse thin-axon neurons, suggesting that stimulation-induced energy demand is met rather by neuronal processes that are independent of mitochondrial abundance to maintain efficient information processing.

item.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

item.title: Resting-state functional brain changes in temporal lobe epilepsy with comorbid depression: A meta-analysis.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Objective To compare the differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those with temporal lobe epilepsy without depressive disorder (TLE-ND) via a meta‑analysis of resting‑state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) studies, and to explore the functional brain activity features associated with depressive symptoms. Methods Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data from database inception to September 2026 to identify cross-sectional studies comparing rs-fMRI-derived differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those without depressive disorder (TLE-ND). Eligible rs-fMRI metrics included regional brain activity indices and functional connectivity indices. A meta-analysis of studies reporting regional brain activity indices was performed using anisotropic effect-size signed differential mapping (AES-SDM). Due to their limited number, studies reporting functional connectivity indices were only described narratively. Study selection and data extraction were then completed, and a voxel-based meta-analysis of the included studies was performed with AES-SDM. Results A total of six studies yielding nine datasets met the inclusion criteria, involving 100 patients with TLE-D and 108 patients with TLE-ND. Meta-analysis showed that, compared with the TLE-ND group, the TLE-D group had significantly increased spontaneous brain activity in the right precuneus, right angular gyrus, right superior frontal gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus, and left cerebellum (analyzed via AES-SDM with an initial exploratory threshold of uncorrected voxel-level P < 0.005 and cluster size ≥10 voxels, and validated by leave-one-out sensitivity analysis). No brain regions with significantly decreased spontaneous brain activity were detected. Conclusion These exploratory findings suggest that, compared with patients with TLE-ND, patients with TLE-D show distinct patterns of functional brain activity in multiple key nodes of the default mode network, including the precuneus and angular gyrus, as well as in prefrontal-related regions. These differences may provide preliminary neuroimaging evidence for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying depressive symptoms associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.

item.title: Global synchrony moderates sad mood and is associated with emotional Stroop interference and somatic symptoms.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Mood-congruent attention in depression has been studied via emotional interference tasks, including tasks comparing responses to sad and happy stimuli. Mood induction offers a way to experimentally induce sad mood in non-clinical samples and examine its association with subsequent emotional interference, including Sad-Happy interference. Previous studies have separately linked resting-state global neural dynamics (synchrony, metastability) to depressive symptoms and attentional processing. However, whether individual differences in baseline global synchrony and metastability relate to how individuals respond to sad mood remains largely unclear. This study therefore examined the relationship between neural dynamics, sadder mood after induction, and Sad-Happy interference. Depressive symptoms also encompass somatic domains alongside cognitive-affective domains, though these are rarely distinguished in neuroimaging studies. We further examined whether baseline neural dynamics and their association with sadder mood and Sad-Happy interference were related to depressive symptoms (total, cognitive-affective, and somatic). Forty-eight non-clinical individuals completed resting-state neuroimaging, mood induction (sad or non-sad), and an emotional Stroop task. We found in a cross-sectional moderated mediation model that sadder mood after induction was associated with greater interference from sad compared to happy stimuli at medium and high levels of global synchrony, particularly in exploratory path models that included somatic symptoms. Findings suggest that individual differences in resting-state global synchrony may be a neural correlate of sadder mood after induction and Sad-Happy interference in non-clinical individuals. This study offers preliminary associations linking neural dynamics, sad mood, emotional interference, and somatic symptoms, providing insights into the role of neural dynamics in emotional and attentional processing.

item.title: The b-Value Dependence for Higher-Degree Spherical Harmonic Powers of the Diffusion MRI Signal Follows Stick Model Predictions in White Matter.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance in medicine
Purpose To compare the dependence on b-value of the spherical harmonic powers for the diffusion MRI signal in white matter to theoretical predictions from the stick model of water diffusion within axons. Methods Diffusion MRI data were acquired at 3 T in three healthy adults with 10 b-value shells (b = 1000-10 000 s/mm2 ) and 64 directions per shell. For every b-value, the signal was expanded in spherical harmonics for all even degrees l up to l = 6, and the harmonic power for each degree was calculated. These were compared in selected white matter regions of interest to the theoretical predictions of the stick model, which depend on just two adjustable parameters: the intra-axonal diffusivity and an amplitude factor for each degree. The intra-axonal diffusivity was estimated independently using triple diffusion encoding MRI, leaving the amplitude factor as the sole fitting parameter. Results Close agreement between experiment and theory was found for b ≳ 4000 s/mm2 , the threshold where extra-axonal water signal is expected to be strongly suppressed, for total cerebral white matter as well as separately within the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum. These findings extend prior studies that either considered only the l = 0 harmonic power or treated the intra-axonal diffusivity as a fitting parameter. Conclusion In white matter, the b-value dependence of the diffusion MRI signal's even degree spherical harmonic powers up to l = 6 are relatively well-described by the stick model of axons for b ≳ 4000 s/mm2 .

item.title: Early-Life Environmental Exposures and Brain Structure in Schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Schizophrenia is widely considered a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by premorbid alterations in brain structure. Urban upbringing is a well-established environmental risk factor. However, urbanicity is often operationalised using broad population-based measures, leaving unclear which features of urban environments might affect the developing brain. This gap limits progress in understanding the pathways linking urban upbringing to schizophrenia, an increasingly important question as global urbanisation progresses. Cortical gyrification is especially informative in this context, as it is largely established before birth and remains relatively stable thereafter, offering a promising retrospective marker of early-life neurodevelopmental disturbances. Study Design: In this case-control MRI study, we examined whether residential environmental exposures at birth were associated with adult brain structure in 51 individuals with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 88 healthy controls matched for age, sex and socioeconomic status. Birth addresses were linked to geospatial measures of air pollution, green space, built volume, built surface and population density. Study Results: Higher air pollution at birth was associated with lower cortical gyrification in individuals with schizophrenia, but not in healthy controls, particularly in orbitofrontal and inferior frontal regions. No comparable associations were observed for grey matter volume, cortical thickness or surface area. Conclusions: These findings suggest that air pollution at birth may be linked to hypogyria in schizophrenia and provide a potential bridge between epidemiological research on urbanicity and neurodevelopmental models of schizophrenia. In turn, this work provides a critical starting point for future work assessing how early urban environments become biologically embedded in schizophrenia risk.

item.title: Age and sex impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity beyond symptom associations in persistent post-concussive symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
1. Objective to investigate whether resting-state EEG aperiodic parameters (i.e., offset and exponent) are associated with symptom burden and demographic factors in patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) and differ from healthy controls. Methods In this cross-sectional observational study, resting-state eye-closed high-density EEG was recorded in patients with PPCS and in age-matched healthy controls. Aperiodic parameters were extracted from EEG power spectra. In patients, hierarchical multiple linear regression models included age and sex as a base model, with additional demographic and clinical symptoms entered separately. Patient-control differences were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex. Results Seventy patients with PPCS (54 female; 39.57±12.21 y.; 109.5 [76.5; 196] days post-concussion) recruited from a concussion care pathway and 38 healthy controls (17 female; 39.61±13.57 y.) were included. In patients, younger age and male sex were associated with higher offset and exponent values (all p ≤.014). None of the additional demographic and clinical variables improved model fit beyond age and sex (all p ≥.143). After adjustment for age and sex, neither offset ( p =.898) nor exponent ( p =.100) differed between patients and controls. Conclusion Resting-state aperiodic EEG parameters were consistently associated with age and sex, but not with self-reported symptom burden or clinical characteristics in patients with PPCS. Not accounting for these factors may generate apparent group differences attributable, at least in part, to demographic variability. Significance Age and sex are important sources of inter-individual variability in resting-state aperiodic EEG activity and should be systematically considered when investigating such features. Highlights Age and sex significantly impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity. Aperiodic EEG parameters were not associated with symptom burden in persistent post-concussive symptoms. Aperiodic offset and exponent did not differ between patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms and healthy controls after adjustment for age and sex.

item.title: Understanding cognitive function in post-COVID-19 condition with fatigue: an interdisciplinary multimodal investigation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Lingering cognitive symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) continue to challenge our understanding, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary research. We investigated whether individuals with PCC and fatigue differ from matched controls across neurocognitive, neuroimaging, and immunological measures, integrating these findings with qualitative phenomenological analyses through multimodal cross-analysis. Individuals with PCC and clinically significant fatigue (n=34), and age-, sex-, and education-matched controls recovered from COVID-19 without PCC (n=37) were included. Assessments encompassed physician evaluation, neuropsychological and functional tests, structural and functional MRI, immunological tests, and qualitative phenomenological analysis of interviews. Data were analyzed using established methods and an interdisciplinary cross-analysis to examine persistent cognitive symptoms in PCC. Group comparisons revealed subtle differences between individuals with PCC and controls, while neurocognitive performance and immunological markers remained within normative ranges. Modest differences in white matter, myelin related, and global brain measures were observed, alongside differences in associations between network connectivity and neurocognitive performance across groups, suggesting reduced network resilience rather than domain specific deficits. This pattern resonated with qualitative phenomenological findings: altered experiences of concentrating and difficulties to execute decisions and actions, despite preserved performance on standard neurocognitive tests. These findings suggest that cognitive symptoms in post-COVID-19 fatigue are associated with subtle neurobiological alterations not captured by standard cognitive assessments. In this highly fatigued sample, converging neuroimaging, neurocognitive and immunological findings point toward reduced network efficiency rather than overt cognitive impairment. Qualitative phenomenological analysis further highlighted altered modes of being in the world characterized by increased cognitive effort and difficulties executing decisions and actions.

item.title: Post-Learning Reactivation of Memories for Naturalistic Continuous Experiences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories are not static records of the past; rather, the act of remembering can change how an event is recalled. Intriguingly, several studies also suggest that memories may be reactivated during rest. However, reactivation has largely been studied for spatial tasks and discrete stimuli, and we know little about whether spontaneous reactivation occurs for long timescale naturalistic events and how reactivation affects retention. Using fMRI, we show that neural activity patterns in the hippocampus and the Default Mode Network during encoding of narrative events were spontaneously reactivated during rest. Contrary to predictions, reactivation did not strengthen recall of movie details, and instead exploratory analyses suggested that reactivation in the hippocampus was associated with more gist-like recall one week later. These findings support the idea that memories for complex events may be spontaneously reactivated, but they suggest that rather than simply strengthening episodic memories, reactivation might help transform them.

item.title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals altered developmental trajectories of functional network organisation associated with adolescent cannabis use
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a critical period of brain development during which the endocannabinoid system continues to mature. These developmental changes may contribute to age-related differences in the association between cannabis use and large-scale functional network organisation, yet this association remains incompletely characterised. We hypothesised that regular cannabis use would be associated with differential one-year changes in resting-state functional connectivity between adolescents and adults. Resting-state fMRI data at two time points, one year apart, were analysed from 66 participants (31 aged 16-17 years; 35 aged 26-29 years) including 29 with regular cannabis use and 37 age-matched cannabis-naive controls. Seed-to-voxel analyses examined longitudinal changes in functional connectivity across age and cannabis-use groups. Year change, age by user-group interactions were identified in salience and default mode network connectivity, including divergent changes in anticorrelations with medial prefrontal, thalamic, cerebellar and juxtapositional regions. Directionality of effects differed by network and region. Additional main effects of user group were observed for executive control and associative striatal connectivity, with the cannabis-use group showing decreased positive connectivity and reduced anticorrelation, respectively. Changes in functional connectivity were developmentally dissociable and predominantly observed in regions contributing to attentional and transmodal processing. These findings suggest that cannabis may be associated with alterations in the maturational refinement of higher-order neural systems, potentially reflecting age-related differences in neurobiological sensitivity to cannabis exposure. Considering developmental stage may therefore be important for characterising cannabis-related neurobiological differences and may have implications for understanding age-dependent vulnerability to cannabis-related psychiatric outcomes.

item.title: Altered intersubject variability of functional connectivity in gray and white matter underlying neurocognition and genetic profiles in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an autoimmune disease that causes inflammatory damage to the central nervous system. While alterations in functional connectivity have been reported in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, changes in intersubject variability of functional connectivity within gray matter and white matter are not yet understood. A total of 66 patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and 71 healthy controls were recruited. We compared intersubject variability of functional connectivity between patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and healthy controls and performed subgroup analyses comparing neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder patients with and without a history of optic neuritis. We also examined the associations between intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and disease duration, clinical disability, and cognitive scores. We combined our imaging results with those of the Allen Human Brain Atlas to conduct transcriptome-neuroimaging association analyses, identified gene expression profiles linked to intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and characterized their potential biological functions. Compared with healthy controls, patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder showed widespread increases in intersubject variability of functional connectivity. Notable gray matter alterations included the precentral and postcentral gyri; extensive occipital areas; and the insula, putamen, and thalamus. The corresponding white matter changes involved the fornix, corticospinal tract, widespread corona radiata, cingulum, and uncinate fasciculus. Compared with patients without optic neuritis, the optic neuritis subgroup exhibited distinct intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations in specific regions, such as the inferior parietal lobule, angular gyrus, thalamus, fornix, and internal capsule. Clinically, only white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlated significantly with physical disability and cognitive processing speed and was not significantly associated with disease duration. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that genes positively associated with white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in synaptic plasticity and cognition, while negatively associated genes were enriched in oxidative stress. Additionally, genes positively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in myelination and lipid biosynthesis, whereas genes negatively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were involved in synapse organization. In conclusion, our study revealed alterations in gray matter- and white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity across neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and clinical subtypes. We demonstrate that changes in white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlate with clinical disability and neurocognition. Linking these connectivity patterns with gene expression profiles may provide insights into the underlying pathophysiology of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

item.title: Mapping Lifespan Functional Connectivity with Vision Transformer and Attention-Guided Trajectory Analysis.
item.description:
International journal of neural systems
Brain aging involves widespread reorganization of functional networks, yet characterizing these changes across the lifespan remains challenging. This study presents an innovative application of a Vision Transformer (ViT) to resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) functional connectivity for age group classification using the Human Connectome Project (HCP) Lifespan datasets. A ViT model was fine-tuned on [Formula: see text] ROI-to-ROI connectivity matrices to perform three binary age group classifications (Young versus Old, Adult versus Aging, Young versus Aging). The model achieved accuracies of 91%, 71%, and 93%, respectively, under five-fold cross-validation. To interpret model decisions, attention weight maps from the final transformer encoder layer were extracted using attention rollout and thresholded with a scree plot analysis, identifying 48 high-salience connections across 28 brain regions. These features were analyzed across the lifespan using generalized additive models (GAM), and k-means clustering of the trajectories revealed three dominant lifespan connectivity patterns: Age-Declining, Mid-Life Peaking, and Age-Increasing. This study demonstrates the viability of the ViT for functional connectome analysis and shows that attention-based interpretability combined with GAM trajectory analysis can enrich insights into age-related changes in brain network connectivity, offering a framework for interpretable brain-age modeling.

item.title: Pain mechanisms in trigeminal neuralgia: From peripheral pathology to brain network reorganization and neurosurgical implications.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
Objectives Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) involves peripheral neurovascular pathology and may also be associated with maladaptive neuroplastic changes in central nervous system networks. This review synthesizes evidence on peripheral and central pain mechanisms, neuroimaging biomarkers, molecular and transcriptomic correlates, and neurosurgical implications, including emerging neuromodulation strategies. Materials and methods This narrative review drew on topic-oriented searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science conducted between June 27 and July 5, 2026, covering literature published through June 2026. Supplementary targeted searches and reference-list screening were used to identify relevant publications. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively. Results Evidence supports a multilevel model of TN involving peripheral pathology and central neuroplastic changes. Neuroimaging studies report structural and functional alterations in sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and default mode networks, alongside disrupted structure-function coupling. Partial restoration of functional connectivity after neurosurgical treatment has been reported, although outcomes vary. Transcriptomic findings link imaging abnormalities to genes involved in ion channel function, synaptic signaling, neuroinflammation, and energy metabolism but remain hypothesis-generating. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may provide short-term analgesic benefit; however, evidence is limited and heterogeneous. Conclusions TN may be understood as a disorder involving interactions between peripheral pathology and central nervous system reorganization. Integrating neuroimaging and molecular evidence may inform future patient stratification and neurosurgical decision-making. Individualized neuromodulation remains investigational and requires further clinical validation.

item.title: Visual-linguistic cues in manual communication: Neural and behavioral responses to Mouthings in sign-naïve perception.
item.description:
Brain and language
Gesture serves as a foundational modality for conveying event structure, providing critical visual information about transitivity and participant roles. Sign languages integrate manual (hand-based) and non-manual (face, torso, head) articulations to encode complex linguistic information. Among these, mouth movements provide phonological and lexical cues, but their role in sign-naïve individuals remains underexplored. This study investigates how sign-naïve individuals process non-manual markers (mouthings) in unfamiliar signed verbs, to explore how linguistic information is extracted from visual stimuli sharing properties with both gesture and sign language. Using EEG, we examined whether lip-reading functions as a linguistic cue or a general perceptual enhancement in non-signers viewing Austrian Sign Language (ÖGS) and non-ÖGS stimuli. Findings reveal distinct neural signatures for manual signs presented with and without congruent mouthings. An early posterior negativity followed by a late posterior positivity suggests that mouthings facilitate lexical access by providing phonological cues that activate stored lexical representations. Conversely, stimuli without mouthings elicited increased anterior activity, reflecting heightened cognitive control demands. Further, telic verbs, which inherently encode event endpoints, showed earlier and stronger facilitation from congruent mouthings compared to atelic verbs. These findings align with the Event Visibility Hypothesis and reinforce the role of visual cues in linguistic comprehension.

item.title: Impact of clinical risk factors on white matter microstructure in preterm-born infants: investigation with diffusion MRI and tractography at term-equivalent age.
item.description:
Journal of neural transmission (Vienna, Austria : 1996)
Premature birth occurs during a phase of intense brain maturation, making white matter (WM) particularly vulnerable to injury. Beyond major lesions, subtle and widespread microstructural alterations also contribute to later neurodevelopmental impairments. We aimed to characterize the impact of key clinical risk factors on global and tract-specific WM microstructure at term-equivalent age (TEA), using 3T-diffusion-MRI data of 111 infants born before 33 weeks of gestation. We implemented a tractography pipeline adapted for use in infants with heterogeneous brain anatomy, including macroscopic abnormalities and lesions, and extracted diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics in sensorimotor tracts: corticospinal tract (CST), superior thalamic radiation (STR), frontal aslant tract (FAT), forceps minor (FMI) and middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP). Associations with risk factors were assessed accounting for age at MRI or global WM microstructure. Tractography succeeded in most infants despite marked anatomical variability and/or overt lesions. Being a male, small for gestational age (SGA) at birth, encountering sepsis and having severe Kidokoro radiological score for WM were associated with altered global WM metrics. At the tract level, CST and STR showed the strongest susceptibility to SGA, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and Kidokoro score. In contrast, associations after adjustment for global WM microstructure suggested that FAT might be less vulnerable than other tracts to extreme prematurity, SGA and invasive ventilation. Findings were partially replicated in infants without macroscopic abnormalities, supporting the presence of WM dysmaturation even in the absence of visible injury. DTI metrics thus provide tract-specific biomarkers of early WM microstructure in preterm infants, which are sensitive to risk factors and could inform targeted prevention and intervention.
